tone: Pathfinder player advising another player; direct, concrete, non-statistical

instructions.capability: Use match when fit >= 0.72 and tension when fit < 0.45.
instructions.directional: Choose the candidateBand from catalogue score: low 1-4, middle 5-6, high 7-10. Use its match text when fit >= 0.72 and tension text when fit < 0.45.
instructions.categorical: Use match for an overlapping preferred value and tension only when the preference is active but no selected value overlaps.
instructions.selection: Lead with at most two highest-weight matches. Add at most one criterion tension after the profile-specific tradeoff. Never expose criterion IDs, scores, weights or percentages.
instructions.variation: Do not repeat the same criterion sentence twice in one shortlist. Profile-specific summary and tradeoff remain the primary source; these fragments explain why that profile answers this player's preferences.

low.match: You want to be close enough to meet the enemy face to face, and this path is built to work there.
low.tension: This path expects you to solve most fights from close quarters, rather than from the safer distance you prefer.

middle.match: You want room to shift between close and ranged fighting, and this path does not lock you into one distance.
middle.tension: Its flexible fighting distance is less committed than the position you had in mind.

high.match: You would rather control the fight from range, and this path can make distance its normal place in battle.
high.tension: This path wants to operate at range, rather than in the close fighting you pictured.

low.match: You want skill, steel and physical technique to do the real work, which is exactly where this path puts its strength.
low.tension: Weapons and physical technique carry this path; magic will not be the main answer you are looking for.

middle.match: You want weapons and magic to feel like parts of the same fighting style, and this path lives in that middle ground.
middle.tension: Its martial and magical sides share the spotlight, instead of committing fully to the side you favour.

high.match: You want magic to be the character's main source of power and answers, and this path gives it that role.
high.tension: Magic drives this path far more than weapon mastery, which pulls it away from your martial idea.

low.match: You want to perfect a distinctive plan, and this path rewards committing to its speciality.
low.tension: This is a focused specialist; it will not keep as many different answers open as you requested.

middle.match: You want a clear signature plan without being helpless when it fails, and this path keeps some alternatives ready.
middle.tension: It splits the difference between specialisation and breadth, rather than embracing your stronger preference.

high.match: You want a broad toolbox and the freedom to change answers with the situation, which is one of this path's strengths.
high.tension: Its breadth comes at the cost of the tight, perfected speciality you wanted.

low.match: You want a dependable turn that stays quick at the table, and this path can rely on a repeatable plan.
low.tension: Its turns tend to repeat a reliable routine, with fewer situational choices than you enjoy.

middle.match: You want a reliable core with a few meaningful decisions around it, and this path strikes that balance.
middle.tension: Its mix of routine and tactical choice is less decisive than the style you asked for.

high.match: You enjoy reading the fight and choosing among several useful actions, and this path gives you those decisions.
high.tension: This path asks for more turn-by-turn judgement than the straightforward routine you prefer.

low.match: You want a character whose main plan works without waiting for allies to set it up, and this path is largely self-contained.
low.tension: This path is more self-contained than the coordinated team play you want.

middle.match: You want to function alone while still gaining something from teamwork, and this path can do both.
middle.tension: It sits between independence and coordination instead of leaning as strongly as you prefer.

high.match: You want allies to combine plans and make one another stronger, and this path gains real value from coordination.
high.tension: This path depends more on allied positioning or cooperation than your independent concept suggests.

low.match: You want the focus to remain on your own character, and this path does not make a companion central to play.
low.tension: A companion is not central here, so it misses the partnership at the heart of your idea.

middle.match: You are open to a familiar or occasional helper without sharing the whole character with it, which suits this path.
middle.tension: Its companion presence is secondary, not as absent or as central as you requested.

high.match: You want a companion to feel like a true partner rather than a decorative extra, and this path makes room for that bond.
high.tension: A companion is a major part of this path, adding attention and responsibility you did not want.

low.match: You would rather start adventuring than rebuild a daily loadout, and this path keeps preparation light.
low.tension: This path offers little daily preparation, so you lose the planning game you wanted.

middle.match: You are comfortable making a few plans without preparing every answer in advance, and this path stays manageable.
middle.tension: Its preparation sits in the middle, rather than matching your stronger preference for spontaneity or detailed planning.

high.match: You enjoy choosing the right tools before the day begins, and this path rewards that preparation.
high.tension: This path asks for more daily preparation than you said you would enjoy.

low.match: You want your contribution to remain dependable through a long day, and this path leans on steady power.
low.tension: Its power is steady rather than explosive, so it offers fewer of the dramatic limited bursts you enjoy.

middle.match: You want a reliable baseline with stronger moments held in reserve, and this path supports that rhythm.
middle.tension: Its mix of steady and limited power is less committed than the rhythm you wanted.

high.match: You enjoy choosing the right moment to spend a powerful limited resource, and this path delivers those peaks.
high.tension: Its best moments rely on limited bursts, which may feel less dependable across the day than you prefer.

low.match: You want a forgiving character that can recover from imperfect choices, and this path gives you a safer margin.
low.tension: This path is safer and more forgiving than the high-risk play you find exciting.

middle.match: You want meaningful risks without making every mistake disastrous, and this path keeps the stakes controlled.
middle.tension: It occupies a middle ground between safety and risk rather than matching your stronger preference.

high.match: You enjoy committing to dangerous plays for a larger payoff, and this path rewards that appetite for risk.
high.tension: Its stronger plays carry more risk and punishment than the forgiving experience you asked for.

low.match: You want influence that can pass unnoticed—through guile, positioning or quiet magic—and this path can work that way.
low.tension: Its power is subtle and indirect, rather than producing the obvious battlefield presence you pictured.

middle.match: You want both quiet solutions and visible impact when the moment calls for it, and this path can move between them.
middle.tension: It mixes subtle and overt tools instead of committing to the presentation you prefer.

high.match: You want everyone at the table to feel when your character changes the fight, and this path makes its impact obvious.
high.tension: Its power is overt and hard to hide, which works against the understated character you described.

low.match: You want to reach a satisfying character without solving a puzzle at every level, and this path is straightforward to build.
low.tension: Its build offers fewer interlocking choices than the character-building depth you enjoy.

middle.match: You want meaningful build choices without needing a guide for every decision, and this path stays in that range.
middle.tension: Its build complexity sits between the simple or deeply optimised experience you asked for.

high.match: You enjoy shaping a character through many connected choices, and this path gives you plenty to tune.
high.tension: This path demands more planning and connected build decisions than you said you wanted.

low.match: You want turns that resolve cleanly and quickly, and this path usually has an obvious useful action.
low.tension: Its turns offer fewer interacting decisions than the tactical play you enjoy.

middle.match: You want a handful of meaningful options without slowing every round, and this path keeps that balance.
middle.tension: Its turn complexity lands between simple and intricate rather than at your preferred extreme.

high.match: You enjoy weighing several effects, targets and timings each round, and this path gives you that tactical density.
high.tension: Its turns ask you to track and compare more options than the quick play you prefer.

low.match: You would rather watch the battlefield than several counters, and this path keeps resource tracking light.
low.tension: It has little resource bookkeeping, so it may feel too plain if managing several moving parts is part of the fun for you.

middle.match: You are comfortable tracking a few important resources without turning the sheet into an accounting exercise.
middle.tension: Its moderate bookkeeping does not lean as far toward simplicity or resource play as you requested.

high.match: You enjoy deciding how to spend several pools, durations or limited uses, and this path rewards that attention.
high.tension: This path brings more pools, durations or limited uses than you want to manage.

low.match: You want the character to work well with the core rules alone, and this path does not demand specialist system knowledge.
low.tension: It leaves less room to exploit deep rules knowledge than you would enjoy.

middle.match: You want to learn a few useful interactions without needing encyclopedic system knowledge, and this path fits that level.
middle.tension: Its rules demands sit between beginner-friendly and expert-facing rather than matching your preference exactly.

high.match: You enjoy finding value in precise wording and system interactions, and this path rewards knowing the rules deeply.
high.tension: This path expects more rules knowledge and judgement than the accessible experience you requested.

low.match: You want to run one character cleanly, and this path rarely adds another stat block or set of actions.
low.tension: It keeps play to one main character, so it misses the extra creatures you wanted to command.

middle.match: You are comfortable with an occasional helper without running a second full character every round.
middle.tension: Its extra-creature workload is neither absent nor central, unlike the clearer preference you expressed.

high.match: You enjoy directing companions or summoned creatures as part of your turn, and this path embraces that workload.
high.tension: This path regularly asks you to manage extra creatures, actions or stat blocks you would rather avoid.

low.match: You want room to make personal choices without accidentally breaking the character, and this path is forgiving.
low.tension: Its forgiving build leaves fewer consequential choices for an optimiser who enjoys walking a narrow line.

middle.match: You want choices to matter without one imperfect pick ruining the concept, and this path offers that middle ground.
middle.tension: Its tolerance for imperfect choices is less extreme than the forgiving or demanding build you requested.

high.match: You enjoy a build where careful choices create a noticeably stronger result, and this path rewards precision.
high.tension: Poorly connected choices can cost this path dearly, making it less forgiving than you asked for.

low.match: You want signature gear to be part of the fantasy and fighting style, and this path makes equipment matter.
low.tension: This path relies heavily on the right equipment, which conflicts with the self-sufficient character you pictured.

middle.match: You are happy for gear to matter without letting one item define the whole character, and this path stays balanced.
middle.tension: Its relationship with equipment is less decisive than the gear-heavy or gear-light style you requested.

high.match: You want your core abilities to remain yours even when equipment is scarce, and this path is unusually self-sufficient.
high.tension: This path is less defined by weapons and gear than the equipment-centred fantasy you wanted.

low.match: You like the identity of a dedicated hunter whose best tools are aimed at particular enemies, and this path rewards that focus.
low.tension: Its strongest tricks are specialised against particular foes, rather than working reliably against almost anyone.

middle.match: You want a speciality without becoming irrelevant outside it, and this path keeps enough broadly useful tools.
middle.tension: It balances specialised and general tools rather than leaning as strongly as you prefer.

high.match: You want your defining abilities to work in most encounters, and this path is not tied tightly to one kind of enemy.
high.tension: Its broad tools offer less of the focused monster-hunter identity you wanted.

low.match: You want a familiar set of spells you can master rather than a new catalogue every morning, and this path keeps its repertoire focused.
low.tension: Its spell access is narrow and relatively fixed, so it cannot provide the changing toolbox you requested.

middle.match: You want a recognisable magical repertoire with some room to adapt, and this path gives you both.
middle.tension: Its spell access sits between a fixed repertoire and a vast changing toolbox rather than at your preferred end.

high.match: You want to choose from a broad magical toolbox and change answers as the adventure changes, which is a defining strength here.
high.tension: Its enormous spell access brings more choice and preparation than the compact repertoire you wanted.

low.match: You want the character to rest mainly on one defining ability score, and this path keeps its demands focused.
low.tension: This path concentrates on one main ability more than the broadly talented character you imagined.

middle.match: You are comfortable supporting one key ability with a second useful strength, and this path asks for about that much.
middle.tension: Its ability demands are neither tightly focused nor broadly spread enough to match your preference exactly.

high.match: You enjoy balancing several strong abilities to make the whole concept work, and this path rewards that investment.
high.tension: This path pulls your ability scores in several directions, making it harder to excel with the focused build you wanted.

low.match: You want the character's principles to remain your roleplaying choice, and this path leaves that freedom in your hands.
low.tension: This path offers personal freedom rather than the oath-bound identity at the centre of your idea.

middle.match: You want strong principles without letting a formal code define every decision, and this path leaves room for both.
middle.tension: Its relationship with codes and duty is less decisive than the freedom or sworn identity you requested.

high.match: You want an oath, discipline or calling to shape who the character is, and this path makes that commitment meaningful.
high.tension: A code or strict calling shapes this path more strongly than the personal freedom you prefer.

low.match: You want beliefs to guide roleplay without risking the character's class powers, and this path keeps those consequences light or absent.
low.tension: Its principles carry little mechanical risk, so it may not deliver the meaningful consequences you welcome.

middle.match: You accept that conduct can matter mechanically, provided one mistake does not erase the character, and this path stays near that balance.
middle.tension: Its conduct consequences are less clearly light or severe than the experience you asked for.

high.match: You welcome a character whose powers and principles are genuinely linked, and this path treats that bond seriously.
high.tension: Breaking this path's obligations can cost real class power, which is harsher than you want from roleplaying choices.

low.match: You want to decide whom the character serves, if anyone, and this path works well as a free agent.
low.tension: This path is largely independent, so it does not provide the order, faith or institution you wanted to belong to.

middle.match: You want ties to a cause or community without surrendering the character's independence, and this path allows that balance.
middle.tension: Its institutional ties are less decisive than the independence or duty you requested.

high.match: You want belonging and duty to an order, faith or calling to shape the story, and this path supports that identity.
high.tension: Duty to a cause or institution weighs more heavily here than the independent character you described.

single-target-damage.match: You want to bring down the one enemy that matters most, and this path can concentrate serious pressure on a single target.
single-target-damage.tension: It is not especially good at focusing down one dangerous enemy, so that job may fall to someone else.

area-damage.match: You want to punish groups rather than trade attacks one enemy at a time, and this path can threaten a wide part of the battlefield.
area-damage.tension: Its damage is mostly focused or limited in area, so crowds are not where it shines.

crowd-control.match: You want to decide where enemies can move and whether they get to act, and this path can reshape the fight around that goal.
crowd-control.tension: It has few reliable ways to lock down enemies or reshape the battlefield.

soft-disruption.match: You want to spoil enemy plans through penalties, positioning and interference, even when a full shutdown is not available.
soft-disruption.tension: It offers little repeatable interference beyond dealing damage or using ordinary attacks.

ally-buffing.match: You enjoy making the whole party hit harder, move better or succeed more often, and this path can raise everyone around it.
ally-buffing.tension: It contributes little direct enhancement to its allies, so support will not be a defining part of play.

healing-recovery.match: You want to restore allies and keep an adventuring day alive after things go wrong, and this path brings real recovery tools.
healing-recovery.tension: Its healing and recovery options are limited, so it cannot comfortably carry that party responsibility.

damage-prevention.match: You would rather stop harm before the hit lands than repair it afterwards, and this path has tools for doing exactly that.
damage-prevention.tension: It tends to answer damage after the fact—or not at all—rather than preventing it reliably.

protect-allies.match: You want to make attacking your companions difficult or costly, and this path can take an active protector's role.
protect-allies.tension: Being personally tough does not make this path a true defender; it has limited ways to keep attacks away from allies.

personal-durability.match: You want to stay standing when enemies turn their attention on you, and this path has the resilience to take that pressure.
personal-durability.tension: It depends more on avoiding danger than absorbing it, so mistakes or focused attacks can be punishing.

mobility.match: You want to change position freely and reach the part of the fight that matters, and this path supports active movement.
mobility.tension: Its movement tools are ordinary or limited, so terrain and enemy positioning can dictate its options.

stealth-infiltration.match: You want to enter unseen, choose the moment and leave without raising the alarm, and this path is comfortable in that role.
stealth-infiltration.tension: It offers little built-in help with remaining unseen or infiltrating protected places.

traps-locks.match: You want the party to trust you with locks, traps and protected mechanisms, and this path can genuinely own that job.
traps-locks.tension: It is not equipped to be the party's answer to traps and locks without substantial outside investment.

social-influence.match: You want conversations to change what the party can achieve, and this path gives you the presence and tools to influence people.
social-influence.tension: It receives little help with persuasion or social leverage, so that part of the concept would rely mostly on personal investment.

intimidation.match: You want fear and force of personality to open doors or break enemy nerve, and this path can turn menace into a real tool.
intimidation.tension: Intimidation is not naturally supported here, so winning through fear would need extra investment.

knowledge-investigation.match: You want to uncover what is really happening and know which answer fits the problem, and this path supports that investigative role.
knowledge-investigation.tension: It brings little built-in knowledge or investigative depth, leaving those answers to other party members.

wilderness.match: You want the character to feel at home beyond roads and cities, and this path contributes naturally to wilderness travel and survival.
wilderness.tension: It offers little special help in the wilderness, so exploration would depend on skills chosen outside its main strengths.

magical-utility.match: You want magic to solve strange problems that weapons and ordinary skills cannot, and this path keeps those answers available.
magical-utility.tension: Its magic offers little broad utility, so unusual obstacles may sit outside the character's toolkit.

summoning-minions.match: You enjoy bringing new bodies and abilities onto the field, and this path can make summoned allies part of its plan.
summoning-minions.tension: Summoned creatures are absent or peripheral here, so it will not deliver the minion-based play you requested.

combat-manoeuvres.match: You want to trip, reposition or physically disable enemies instead of only trading damage, and this path supports those tactics.
combat-manoeuvres.tension: It has little special support for combat manoeuvres, making those tactics less dependable against serious opponents.

resource-endurance.match: You want to remain useful after several encounters, and this path keeps a meaningful contribution when limited resources run low.
resource-endurance.tension: Its signature contribution fades as daily resources are spent, so a long adventuring day can expose it.

melee-weapon-effectiveness.match: You want weapon attacks in close combat to remain a serious answer, and this path can win fights through them.
melee-weapon-effectiveness.tension: Its melee weapon attacks are secondary or poorly supported, so standing toe to toe is not its natural solution.

ranged-weapon-effectiveness.match: You want ranged weapon attacks to be more than a fallback, and this path can build its combat identity around them.
ranged-weapon-effectiveness.tension: It has little support for winning fights with ranged weapons.

offensive-spellcasting.match: You want spells that directly hurt enemies, and this path can make offensive casting a central threat.
offensive-spellcasting.tension: Its spellcasting is not well suited to dealing direct magical damage.

defensive-magic.match: You want magic to create safety through wards, concealment, resistance or control, and this path has those defensive answers.
defensive-magic.tension: It offers few magical ways to keep danger away from itself or the party.

condition-removal.match: You want to get allies back into the fight when poison, curses or disabling effects take hold, and this path can carry that responsibility.
condition-removal.tension: It has limited answers to harmful conditions, so the party will still need another source of recovery.

dispelling-countermagic.match: You want to answer enemy magic directly, and this path can unravel spells and magical protections.
dispelling-countermagic.tension: It has few dependable tools for dispelling or countering hostile magic.

shapeshifting-transformation.match: You want changing form to alter what the character can do, and transformation is a meaningful part of this path.
shapeshifting-transformation.tension: Transformation is absent or minor here, so it does not fulfil a shapeshifter fantasy.

natural-weapon-combat.match: You want claws, bites or another transformed body to be a genuine fighting style, and this path can support it.
natural-weapon-combat.tension: Natural attacks are not a serious combat plan for this path without building far outside its strengths.

mounted-combat.match: You want mount and rider to fight as a single unit, and this path can support that battlefield identity.
mounted-combat.tension: Mounted combat receives little direct support here, even if the character can acquire a mount by other means.

skill-breadth.match: You want useful answers after initiative ends as well as during combat, and this path can cover a broad range of skills.
skill-breadth.tension: Its skill coverage is narrow, so much of the character's value will stay inside its main speciality.

first-round-impact.match: You want to seize momentum before the enemy settles into the fight, and this path can matter immediately.
first-round-impact.tension: It often needs setup or the right circumstances before its strongest contribution appears.

armour-defence.match: You want solid armour to be a dependable part of staying alive, and this path makes good use of it.
armour-defence.tension: Armour is light, restricted or secondary here, so defence comes from other tools.

shield-combat.match: You want a shield to shape both defence and fighting style, and this path can make it more than passive equipment.
shield-combat.tension: A shield is unsupported or conflicts with the path's normal combat rhythm.

casting-level.minor: You want a touch of magic without turning the character into a dedicated caster.
casting-level.4-level: You want limited spellcasting to support a primarily martial or skill-based role.
casting-level.6-level: You want magic and another play style to share the character rather than one replacing the other.
casting-level.9-level/full: You want full spell progression and the depth of magic that comes with it.

casting-method.none: You do not want daily spell decisions to define play.
casting-method.prepared: You enjoy choosing the right spells for the day ahead.
casting-method.spontaneous: You prefer a familiar repertoire you can cast without preparing individual spells.
casting-method.flexible/hybrid: You want casting that can shift between prepared planning and flexible use.
casting-method.item-mediated: You like turning scrolls, wands and other magical items into part of the character's spell access.
casting-method.spontaneous-domain: You want domain magic available with spontaneous freedom.
casting-method.reusable-hexes: You like magical tricks that can be used repeatedly instead of spending a spell slot each time.

magic-identity.none: You want the character's identity to remain non-magical.
magic-identity.arcane: You want learned or arcane power to define the character's magic.
magic-identity.divine: You want divine power and sacred magic at the heart of the concept.
magic-identity.nature: You want magic rooted in the natural world.
magic-identity.psychic/occult: You want strange mental or occult power rather than conventional spellcraft.
magic-identity.alchemical: You want formulae, mixtures and physical experimentation to explain the character's power.
magic-identity.supernatural/non-spell: You want extraordinary powers that do not feel like ordinary spellcasting.
magic-identity.fey: You want fey influence, enchantment and otherworldly whimsy in the character's magic.
magic-identity.elemental: You want the raw elements to shape the character's magical identity.
magic-identity.bloodline: You want magic to feel inherited, instinctive and personal.
magic-identity.curse: You want curses and unsettling magic to be part of the character's signature.
magic-identity.divine-imitation: You like the fantasy of using arcane talent to imitate or exploit divine magic.
magic-identity.reincarnation: You want death, renewal and returning in a new form to define the character's supernatural story.

primary-delivery.weapon: You want the character's signature effects to arrive through a weapon.
primary-delivery.natural attacks: You want the character's own transformed or monstrous body to deliver its attacks.
primary-delivery.ranged weapon: You want bows or other ranged weapons to carry the main combat plan.
primary-delivery.spell: You want spells themselves to be the character's main way of affecting a fight.
primary-delivery.bomb: You want prepared explosives or similar thrown creations to deliver the character's power.
primary-delivery.companion: You want a companion to carry a meaningful share of the character's contribution.
primary-delivery.manoeuvre: You want trips, repositioning and physical control to define how the character fights.
primary-delivery.hex: You want repeatable hexes or curses to be the character's signature delivery method.

armour-preference.unarmoured: You want the character to fight without relying on armour.
armour-preference.light: You prefer light armour that leaves movement and agility intact.
armour-preference.medium: You want a practical balance between protection and mobility.
armour-preference.heavy: You want heavy armour to be visible, dependable and central to the fantasy.
armour-preference.shield-compatible: You want the build to work naturally while carrying a shield.

companion-type.none: You want to manage only your own character.
companion-type.familiar: You want a familiar for personality, scouting or clever utility.
companion-type.animal companion: You want a persistent animal partner with a real battlefield presence.
companion-type.multiple companions: You enjoy directing several persistent creatures rather than one partner.
companion-type.summoned creatures: You prefer calling different temporary creatures as the situation changes.
companion-type.bonded object: You want an important magical object without giving it an independent personality.
companion-type.sentient item: You want a conscious item with its own voice, motives and relationship with the character.

party-contribution.damage: You want the party to feel your contribution through enemies going down.
party-contribution.control: You want to shape enemy movement, actions and choices.
party-contribution.protection: You want to make the whole party harder to hurt.
party-contribution.support: You want allies to succeed because of the advantages you create.
party-contribution.healing: You want to restore allies and keep the group adventuring.
party-contribution.skills: You want practical expertise to solve problems outside direct combat.
party-contribution.information: You want to uncover threats, weaknesses and hidden answers.
party-contribution.exploration: You want to guide the party through travel, terrain and unfamiliar places.

social-style.honest leadership: You want to influence people through credibility, authority and direct leadership.
social-style.charm: You want warmth and personal appeal to open social doors.
social-style.deception: You enjoy changing the situation through lies, disguises and confidence tricks.
social-style.intimidation: You want fear and force of personality to carry conversations.
social-style.performance: You want art, spectacle or performance to be part of social influence.
social-style.no preference: You want freedom to decide the character's social approach through skills and roleplay.

best-overall: This is the clearest match for the character you described.
This path brings the strongest parts of your idea together.
different-approach: This reaches a similar destination from a very different direction.
If you are willing to change the route rather than the goal, this is worth a look.
more-approachable: This keeps much of the fantasy while being easier to build and run.
If you want the concept with fewer moving parts, this is the gentler entry point.
unexpected-fit: This may not be the class you first imagined, but it answers an important part of your concept surprisingly well.
This is the less obvious option—the mechanics fit your idea better than the class name suggests.

specialCaseRules.text: A Druid's bond with nature is a real class obligation: prohibited alignment or conduct can suspend spells and class abilities until atonement.
You choose the deity; the choice is yours, but its alignment and expectations can shape how the character must behave.
Razmir's church defines the published story, but worship and church membership are not mechanical prerequisites of the archetype.
The Black Blade has its own purpose and Ego. That can create conflict, but it is a relationship with an intelligent item—not a code whose breach removes your class powers.
This recommendation assumes you choose an animal companion for Nature Bond, making that partner a much larger part of both the story and your turns.
Always state the parent class in the first sentence; never present an archetype as a standalone class.
